# Implement in kurasu - **Tracker**: an Entire trail per change, created with `entire trail create --no-branch --type feature`. The trail's description holds the change's tasks as a markdown checklist, one `- [ ]` line per task with what it requires. There is no local task list. - **Reaching it**: `entire trail show

--json` reads the description; `entire trail update

--body "…"` writes it, and replaces the whole description, so read it first and write it back whole. - **States**: a task is pending as `- [ ]` and done as `- [x]`. It is marked done when its change is implemented, tested and committed. There is no in-progress state. The trail goes to `--status closed` when its branch is merged. - **Description format**: Entire stores the description as plain text: it drops list dashes, bold, backticks, headings and blank lines, and keeps the `[ ]`/`[x]` marks. It keeps line breaks only when the body is written as a markdown list: write each task as `- [ ] `, with a blank line around the `Tareas` heading line. A body of bare `[ ]` lines comes back as one paragraph. - **Branch**: the trail is created without a branch. Once the change's branch is pushed, and before its pull request is opened, link it with `entire trail link

--branch `. A pull request whose branch belongs to no trail makes Entire create a new trail for it. - **Supervisor session**: the subagents' sessions reach the trail through their commits on the branch; the supervisor's session runs on `main` and does not. When the run ends, attach it with `entire session attach $PI_SESSION_ID --commit `, choosing the branch's last commit that already has a checkpoint (`entire checkpoint list`), so the session joins that checkpoint without rewriting history. It shows on the trail once the branch is linked. - **Closing**: close the trail with `entire trail update

--status closed` once its pull request is merged.

1. **R5, opaque `Write`.**
   - In `packages/core/src/batch.ts`, `Write` is now a branded interface. The core only has a symbol brand and cannot see inside it.
   - `packages/database/src/database.ts` holds one wrap/unwrap pair: `write(statement)` keeps the Drizzle statement in a `WeakMap`, and `batch` unwraps it.
   - `repository.ts` still has its raw `statements` and exposes `writes` through `write`. The one-off statements in `materials`, `users`, `questions` and `sessions` call `write(...)` where they enter a batch.
   - The repo's lint forbids type assertions, so I used the `WeakMap` and no cast. Behaviour is the same.
2. **R12, dark mode.** `FeaturedQuestionsSwitch` uses `border-line` and `text-ink` instead of `border-sand` and `text-coal`. Light mode looks the same, and the title and line read in dark mode.
3. **R7, changelog test.**
   - "featuring a session records nothing" moved to `featured.test.ts`, and the "must run last" comment is gone from `changelog.test.ts`.

# Human review

Verifies the user's own reading of a change and settles it with them. Nothing is edited until they rule on it.

Start one `plannotator review` per repository, backgrounded, all in a single message:

cd {absolute-repo-path} && plannotator review

---
name: "changeset"
description: "Loaded by other skills to establish which change is under review: the repositories, the base it is measured against, and the diff composed from them."
user-invocable: false
---
# Changeset

Defines the change once, so every skill that reasons about one agrees on what it is. A skill that reviews, traces, or reports on a change loads this first.

## Address every repository by path

Collect the absolute path of every repository the change touches. Use `git -C <repo-path>` for every git command and absolute paths for every read.

**Never `cd`.** A foreground `cd` persists across Bash calls, so a later call, especially one of several sent in the same message, runs in whichever repository was entered last and returns its output under the wrong name. Nothing errors, and the output looks plausible.

## Establish the base

The base is the commit you measure the change against. Report it, never assume it silently.

```
bash ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/skills/changeset/scripts/find-base-branch.sh <repo-path>
```

The script fetches and returns, as JSON, the remote branch that the current branch has the fewest commits ahead of. That remote branch is the one the current branch was cut from. It skips the branch's own remote copy. Use its `base_branch` as `origin/<base_branch>`. Do not take the base from `origin/HEAD`, because it can point at a trunk the work did not branch from. When the script errors or returns a branch you cannot account for, ask. **Never guess between `main` and `master`** by checking which exists, because a repository can carry both. Do not fall back to `HEAD~1`.

Two sources reviewing the same work against different bases produce findings you cannot compare. When more than one source is involved, report each one's base.

## Compose the diff

A changeset is composed from these parts, and you decide which are in scope rather than taking a default:

| Part | Command |
|---|---|
| Committed on the branch | `git -C <repo> diff <base>...HEAD` |
| Uncommitted | `git -C <repo> diff HEAD` |
| Untracked | `git -C <repo> status --porcelain` |

Use the three-dot form for the committed part. It shows what the branch added since it diverged and excludes anything that landed on the base meanwhile. Two-dot mixes the two and attributes other people's commits to this change.

Stashed work is not part of the changeset. Neither is work on another branch. Include either only when the user says to, and say in the report that you did.

State the composition you used in one line before presenting anything derived from it, so a wrong scope shows up instead of passing unnoticed.

## Separate introduced from pre-existing

A line inside the diff is not necessarily a change the diff made. Before calling anything introduced, read the base version:

```
git -C <repo-path> show <base>:<path>
```

Compare the behavior, not the text. Code can move, be re-indented, or be extracted without changing what it does, and a symbol can sit untouched while its callers change what they pass it. `git log` and `git show <commit>` settle which commit introduced a line when the base comparison is not enough.

Every claim that something is new, changed, or broken carries this distinction: introduced here, pre-existing, or pre-existing and widened by this change.

# Land

Coordinates the plugin's skills into one process, from open branches to merged pull requests. It merges no pull request and picks no order on its own.

## Step 1: Check the release

Run mahou:release-check on the repositories in scope. Present its release order and wait until the user confirms it or changes it.

A change can break no boundary when it touches one repository and changes no request, response, schema or event that crosses a service boundary. When both hold, say so with the facts that show it, propose skipping mahou:release-check, and give the one-step order. The user confirms the skip and the order together, or asks for the check.

## Step 2: Open the pull requests

Run mahou:create-pull-request once per repository, all together.

Report every PR URL.

## Step 3: Babysit the pull requests

Start one background loop per PR that polls at a fixed interval and exits on the first of these:

- an unresolved review thread appeared, or the review body has a finding without a thread
- the branch fell behind its base
- a check failed
- the PR was merged

```
gh pr view <number> --repo <owner>/<repo> --json state,mergeStateStatus,statusCheckRollup
```

plus the review threads through the GraphQL API (`gh api graphql`, the `reviewThreads` connection of the pull request, reading `isResolved` per thread). `gh pr checks --watch` blocks on checks, but nothing in `gh` blocks on reviews or merges, so the loop polls.

When a loop exits, handle that PR and start its loop again:

- **Review.** Run mahou:address-pr-review on that PR. It settles the findings with the user, applies what they approve, commits, pushes and resolves the threads.
- **Behind its base.** Run mahou:rebase, which never pushes. Report what moved and push once the user confirms.
- **Failed check.** Report the check with its URL and stop for the user.
- **Merged.** Record it.

The user merges the pull request, either in GitHub or by asking you to merge it.

## Step 4: Merge in order

Walk the confirmed order. The release follows each project's own process once its pull request merges; usually the CI publishes the tag on its own. For each repository:

1. Wait until its pull request is merged and the user has confirmed that every repository before it in the order works in production.
2. Watch the CI run the merge triggers:

   ```
   gh run watch <run-id> --repo <owner>/<repo> --exit-status
   ```

   Report the jobs, their conclusions, and the tag when the run publishes one. A failed job stops everything until the user decides.
3. Stop. The next repository starts when the user confirms this one works in production.

## Step 5: Clean up the local checkout

Once every repository has merged and the user has confirmed the last one, clean up each repository's local checkout:

1. Switch to the base branch its pull request merged into, and pull it.
2. Delete the merged local branch with `git -C <repo-path> branch -d <branch>`. `-d` refuses a branch that is not merged. When git refuses, report it and do not force-delete the branch.

Report the branch each repository is on and its new head.

## Step 6: Report

One line per repository: PR, merge, the CI result, and the tag when the project's automation published one. Then stop.

# Create pull request

Opens one pull request from one branch. It merges nothing and decides nothing the repository or the user has not settled.

## Step 1: Resolve the repository and the branch

The repository comes from the argument, or from the working directory. Read the owner and name from the remote, supporting both SSH (`git@github.com:owner/repo.git`) and HTTPS (`https://github.com/owner/repo.git`) forms:

```
git -C <repo-path> remote get-url origin
```

The branch comes from the argument, or from `git -C <repo-path> branch --show-current`. Detached HEAD with no argument: ask for the branch.

## Step 2: Find the base branch

```
bash ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/skills/changeset/scripts/find-base-branch.sh <repo-path>
```

The script fetches, compares the branch against every remote ref except `HEAD` and its own remote copy, and returns as JSON the `base_branch` with the fewest commits ahead of HEAD, the one this branch was most likely forked from, plus its `ahead` and `behind` counts. Distance ties or an unclear picture go to the user with the numbers; never guess between `main` and `master`. State the base you settled on and its ahead/behind counts.

## Step 3: Analyze every commit on the branch

List the commits the branch has over the base (`git log origin/<base>..HEAD`) and read each one's files changed. The pull request reflects the whole branch, not the latest commit. A PR already open for the branch: report its URL and ask whether to update it instead of creating a second one.

## Step 4: Write the title and body

- **Title.** A single commit takes its subject line. Several commits get one descriptive title covering what the branch accomplishes together. Strip conventional-commit prefixes: "Add cycle recommendations" rather than "feat(study plan): add cycle recommendations".
- **Body.** A `## Summary` with two to four factual bullets on what the branch accomplishes, derived only from the commits. No file listing, no test plan section, no validation section.

Show the title, the body and the base, and wait for the user's confirmation before creating anything.

## Step 5: Create and report

```
gh pr create --repo <owner>/<repo> --head <branch> --base <base> --title "<title>" --body "<body>"
```

Report the pull request's URL. Then stop; the review and the merge are not this skill's.

name: terminal-browser
description: A real browser running inside the terminal. It splits the human's terminal pane automatically, so you can show a website side by side with the conversation, render HTML to visualize something, and drive whatever tab is open — snapshot, click, fill, eval — with the `terminal-browser action` subcommand.
---

`terminal-browser open <url>` puts a browser in a terminal pane. On its own it
takes over the current pane. `--split right` (or `down`, `left`, `up`) opens a
new pane beside the human, which is how you show a page next to the
conversation. A path to a local html file works the same as a url, so writing a
page and opening it is a way to show something you built.

`terminal-browser ls` shows the browsers and tabs in this terminal tab, with the
tab ids the other commands take.

`terminal-browser action -- <command>` is an agent-browser compatible CLI for a
tab that is already open. It targets this terminal tab's browser and its active
tab unless you select another one.

When you use the terminal-browser action sub command, the user will visually
see in the browser tab an indication that you are acting on the browser tab. This
will automatically hide after a preset duration, where the countdown resets
everytime terminal-browser action is used. But its a much better experience
for the user if after the last time you plan to use terminal-browser action you
run terminal-browser action done, which immediately clears the indication
that you are using the browser tab

Some pages publish WebMCP tools: named actions with a JSON schema that the
page runs itself. agent-browser announces them when a page has them, and
`terminal-browser action -- webmcp list --json` shows the full schemas. Prefer
`terminal-browser action -- webmcp invoke <tool> --params '<json>'` over
snapshot, click and fill when a tool covers what you need; it is faster and
does not break when the layout changes. Tools can carry annotations. Treat
`readOnly: false` as a change to the user's data and `consequential: true` as
something to confirm with the user before invoking.

$ terminal-browser help
Usage: terminal-browser [url] [options]

  open            Open the browser in a terminal pane
  ls              List running browsers and their tabs
  setup           Configure terminals and agents so terminal-browser works best
  upgrade         Upgrade to the latest release
  new-tab         Open a tab here, and a browser too if there is none
  apps            Lists registered terminal-browser apps
  register-app    Register a terminal-browser application
  unregister-app  Unregister a terminal-browser application
  shutdown        Stop the daemon
  config          Get and set settings and shortcuts
  action          Use the open browser through the agent-browser CLI

terminal-browser <command> --help for one command's options
terminal-browser --version prints the installed version
```

```

Usage: terminal-browser open [url] [options]

Opens the browser in the current pane. Pass --split to open it in a new
split pane instead.

The url can be a normal url, a localhost port, or a path to an html file.

Options:
  --split <direction>   Open in a new pane: right, left, down, up
  --size <fraction>     How much of the space the split takes (0.2 to 0.95)
  --ssh <user@host>     Perform all network requests through a remote server, then
                        proxy the result back to the local terminal-browser instance
  --allow-clipboard-read
                        Lets websites read from clipboard.
  --no-merge            Do not open the terminal-browser instance as a tab in a neighbor terminal-browser


Examples:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Polls PR #19 until a review thread is open, the branch falls behind, a check fails, or it merges.
R=filadd/agentic-engineering-famaf-extension-course
N=19

while true; do
  pr=$(gh pr view $N --repo $R --json state,mergeStateStatus,statusCheckRollup,reviews 2>/dev/null)

  if [ -n "$pr" ]; then
    state=$(jq -r .state <<<"$pr")
    merge=$(jq -r .mergeStateStatus <<<"$pr")
    failed=$(jq -r '[.statusCheckRollup[]? | select(.conclusion=="FAILURE" or .conclusion=="CANCELLED" or .conclusion=="TIMED_OUT")] | length' <<<"$pr")
    reviews=$(jq -r '[.reviews[]? | select(.state=="CHANGES_REQUESTED" or ((.body // "") != ""))] | length' <<<"$pr")
    threads=$(gh api graphql -f query='query { repository(owner:"filadd", name:"agentic-engineering-famaf-extension-course") { pullRequest(number:19) { reviewThreads(first:100) { nodes { isResolved } } } } }' --jq '[.data.repository.pullRequest.reviewThreads.nodes[] | select(.isResolved==false)] | length' 2>/dev/null)

    if [ "$state" = "MERGED" ]; then echo "PR-EVENT merged"; exit 0; fi
    if [ "$state" = "CLOSED" ]; then echo "PR-EVENT closed"; exit 0; fi
    if [ "${threads:-0}" -gt 0 ] || [ "${reviews:-0}" -gt 0 ]; then echo "PR-EVENT review threads=$threads reviews=$reviews"; exit 0; fi
    if [ "$merge" = "BEHIND" ] || [ "$merge" = "DIRTY" ]; then echo "PR-EVENT behind merge=$merge"; exit 0; fi
    if [ "${failed:-0}" -gt 0 ]; then echo "PR-EVENT check-failed count=$failed"; exit 0; fi
  fi

  sleep 60
done

app/package.json:17:    "deploy": "APP_ENV=production varlock run -- pnpm --filter @kurasu/infra deploy",
app/apps/infra/package.json:9:    "deploy": "alchemy deploy --stage prod",
app/apps/infra/package.json:10:    "destroy": "alchemy destroy"
.mahou/wiki/alchemy/local-dev.md:10:- `Website.Vite` passes the dev server only the `VITE_` entries of its `env`, as `import.meta.env.VITE_*` `define`s in Vite's inline config; the Vite process does not get the Worker's other env entries or any per-Worker process variable. The stack gives the web `env: { VITE_API_URL: api.url }` in dev only, and a dev-only plugin in `apps/web/vite.config.ts` (`apiProxy`) reads `config.define["import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL"]` in its `config` hook and sets the proxy target. This works because Vite merges the inline config into the config file's before it runs the plugins' `config` hooks. The value stays out of the deployed web: the build only inlines `VITE_` keys that the props carry, and the production props have none.
.mahou/wiki/alchemy/local-tests.md:5:Answers how integration tests run against a local Alchemy 2 stack: how much state a test file gets, how to start from a clean database with fixtures, how to read and fail the mail a Worker sends, and what cannot be made to fail. The facts come from the alchemy source at 2.0.0-beta.83 (commit 9e3c058) and its issues. kurasu's API suite applies them: it deploys one stage per file, loads the fixtures through `importFiles`, reads the mail from `text/*.txt` and the recipients from the stage's Worker log, makes sends fail with `allowedDestinationAddresses`, and sets `sequence.hooks: "list"`.
.mahou/wiki/alchemy/local-tests.md:9:- `alchemy/Test/Vitest` with `dev: true` deploys the stack once per `Test.make` call, in `beforeAll`, so once per test file.
.mahou/wiki/alchemy/local-tests.md:11:- There is no API to reset a local D1 or R2 between tests. `destroy` keeps the data, because the local `delete` handlers do nothing. To start clean, deploy a new stage (`Test.make({ stage })` or `deploy(Stack, { stage })`) per test file, or delete `.alchemy/local` and `.alchemy/state` between runs.
.mahou/wiki/alchemy/local-tests.md:12:- Migrations apply on every deploy. `D1.Database({ importFiles: ["<fixtures>.sql"] })` runs SQL after the migrations, and skips a file whose hash has not changed. The tests of one file share that data, so each test creates or uses its own records.
.mahou/wiki/alchemy/local-tests.md:15:- To make a send fail without mocks, declare `allowedDestinationAddresses` (or `allowedSenderAddresses`) on `Cloudflare.Email.SendEmail` for the test stage. A send to an address outside the list throws `email to <addr> not allowed`, which reaches the Worker as `SendEmailError`. The list is fixed at deploy time.
.mahou/wiki/alchemy/local-tests.md:17:- Each run of a suite that deploys a stage per file leaves the stages' state, bundles and local data behind. In kurasu's API suite, each run adds about 130 MB to `apps/api/.alchemy`, and nothing removes it.

content.thinking:
I'm tracing how rapid "next" clicks race against each other: each click reads the current slide from the cached session and fires its own PATCH. The concern is that the response for the first click may land after later clicks have already updated the cache, and its onSuccess then overwrites the newer state with stale session data.

Next I'm checking the other race sources: each move pushes a "slide" notice back to the teacher's own socket, which triggers a refetch that can return a stale server value and overwrite the local state. I'm also noting that in-flight refetches are cancelled on mutate, but ones triggered afterward are not, and that concurrent PATCHes can reach the server out of order, leaving the final slide wrong.

I'm weighing a serial queue for the moves, since React Query's `scope` option might run same-scope mutations one after another, and I need to confirm the installed version supports it. A coalescing variant is also worth considering: keep only the latest pending slide while a request is in flight, which cuts five clicks down to about two requests. I'd also stop writing server responses into the cache while newer moves are still pending.

I'm checking whether `isMutating` with a mutation key can serve as the guard, so a refetch doesn't overwrite local state while moves are still pending.

I'm checking whether `isMutating` scoped to the move key can block the refetch while moves are pending. There's also a concern that `onMutate` awaits `cancelQueries` before the optimistic patch lands, so rapid clicks might all compute "next" from the same stale position and collapse into one target.

I'm checking whether `onMutate` runs only once the earlier mutation finishes, since that would delay the optimistic patch. If it does, the local position won't advance on click, so the queue should handle only the network calls while the local state updates synchronously. I'll check the installed TanStack Query version and how `scope` behaves in its source.

content.thinking:
I'm checking how the optimistic updates interact when clicks come in quickly. The immediate local patch is fine, but each server response could overwrite later pending changes with an intermediate state, and rollbacks restore a snapshot from that mutation's own start, which can be stale under rapid clicks. I'm also tracing what happens when the socket "slide" notice invalidates the admin session.

I'm weighing whether a coalescing queue, keeping only the latest pending position, beats queuing every step, since intermediate position updates would make students jump through slides.

I'm sketching three fixes: make the move mutations run serially under one scope, stop server responses from overwriting while a move is pending, and have TeacherSlides keep a local position as the source of truth so the socket refetch can't yank it back.

I'm settling on a design: keep the position locally in TeacherSlides, coalesce pending moves so only the latest one is sent with one request in flight, and drop the optimistic cache patch. Server echoes get ignored while a move is pending, and I'd resync from the server only when idle. Error handling needs a rethink too, since snapshot rollback doesn't hold up under a queue, so I'd refetch the server value and show a toast instead.

content.text:
Your idea is right, but queueing alone won't fix it: the queue only makes the requests go one at a time. The screen also has to keep its own position while the moves are saving, and stop taking the server's answers until the last move lands.

**Why it gets stuck today.** The position comes from the cached session, and each click calculates the next one from it. There are three writers to that cache:

1. **Each click** writes the new position before the request goes out.
2. **Each server response** writes back the position that request saved, in `useMoveSlide.ts`'s `onSuccess`. If you clicked to slide 5 and the answer for slide 3 arrives, the screen goes back to 3.
3. **Each save sends a "slide" notice** back to your own page over the classroom socket, which refetches the session (`invalidate-topic.ts`). That refetch can also bring back an old position.

When a response or a refetch moves the screen back, your next click calculates from that old position. That's what you see as stuck, or as going backwards. A failed move also restores the snapshot it took when you clicked, which with several moves in flight is out of date too.

**What would actually fix it:**

- **The position lives in `TeacherSlides`, not in the cache.** A click moves that position right away and asks for the save. While a move is pending, the screen ignores both what the server answers and what the refetch brings. When nothing is pending, it takes the server's position again, so a move from another teacher tab still shows up.
- **One save at a time, keeping only the last position.** I'd do this rather than queue every step. If you click five times quickly, the first save goes out, and when it answers, only the last position goes out. You make fewer requests, and the students and the "Presentar en otra pestaña" tab don't step through every intermediate slide; they jump to where you stopped. If you want every step to reach the students, the queue can keep all of them, with the same local position.
- **React Query can already run mutations one at a time.** v5.104 has a `scope` option on a mutation, and mutations with the same `scope` run one after another. It's only needed if you pick the full queue; for "keep only the last position", a small ref with the pending position is enough.
- **The optimistic patch and `onSuccess` go away from `useMoveSlide`.** The local position takes their role. If a save fails, the toast stays and the screen goes back to what the server has.

**What the change touches:** `TeacherSlides.tsx` (the local position and the queue) and `useMoveSlide.ts` (no patch, no `onSuccess`). Nothing changes in the API or the student side. I'd add a web test that clicks "Siguiente" several times with the save held, and checks that the position doesn't go back and that only the last position is sent.

Which do you prefer: keep only the last position, or send every step?

I'm weighing whether an optimistic update with cancelling earlier mutations could fix this. React Query can't cancel an in-flight mutation, since `cancelQueries` only applies to queries. Aborting the fetch would stop the client from waiting, but the request may already have reached the server and written the data, and those server writes are what trigger the notices. Abort also wouldn't guarantee the order of writes.

I'm checking whether serialization is needed, since older requests could land after newer ones at the server and leave it on an old position. Keeping the optimistic patch in cache still looks workable if I drop the success write, skip the response and rollback while another move is pending, and stop notice-triggered refetches from overwriting it.

I'm considering whether the mutations can run one at a time, with each one reading the latest slide position from the cache, so queued moves that find their position already sent can skip the request. Since the request can't be cancelled once it's out, the plan is to stop older responses from writing into the cache and to keep the sends serialized.

I'm comparing the two routes: a local state approach that touches two files and leaves classroom invalidation alone, against a cache approach that changes the move hook, the generic rollback, and topic invalidation. The mid-sequence case matters here, since a notice for an earlier move can refetch and overwrite a newer position, so the invalidation path needs a pending-move check either way.

I'm settling on the recommendation now: both routes work, but I lean toward local state since it stays contained in two files and doesn't require changing the generic mutation rollback or the classroom notice handling. content.text:
Yes, it can work through the cache, but "cancelling previous mutations" doesn't exist as such. React Query has no way to cancel a mutation, and aborting the request in the browser doesn't undo a write that already reached the server. It also doesn't fix the order: two requests in flight can reach D1 in any order, so the server could end up on an earlier slide. The moves still have to go one at a time. "Cancelling" really means stopping older answers from writing into the cache.

**What the cache version needs:**

1. **Keep the optimistic patch** in `useMoveSlide`, so each click writes the new position into the cached session and the next click calculates from it.
2. **Drop the `onSuccess` that writes the response back** into the cache. That write is what moves the screen back when an older answer arrives.
3. **Run moves one at a time and send only the latest.** Give the mutation a `scope` per session so React Query queues them. Have the request read the current position from the cache instead of from its own input. When a queued move's turn comes, it sends the latest position, or does nothing if that position was already sent. Five quick clicks end up as at most two requests: the first click and the last position.
4. **Ignore the "slide" notice refetch while a move is pending.** Each save sends a notice back over the socket, and today it refetches the session. If the notice for move 1 arrives while move 2 is pending, the refetch writes slide 1 over your slide 3. `invalidateTopic` would skip the session refetch for `slide` when `queryClient.isMutating({ mutationKey: ["move-slide", sessionId] })` is above zero. The last save's notice still refetches, so the screen ends up on what the server has.
5. **Only roll back when nothing else is pending.** `useApiMutation` restores its snapshot on any failure, and with several moves queued that snapshot is out of date. Either the shared hook gets an option to skip the rollback, or `useMoveSlide` does its own and invalidates the session after a failure.

**Compared with keeping the position in `TeacherSlides`:**
- **Both fix it** and send only the last position.
- **The cache version** keeps one source of truth for the position. It touches `useMoveSlide`, the shared `useApiMutation` (the rollback option) and the classroom's `invalidate-topic`.
- **The local-state version** touches only `TeacherSlides` and `useMoveSlide`, and leaves the shared hook and the notices as they are.

I lean towards the local state because it's contained, but the cache version is sound if it does all five steps above. Which one should I implement?

40:Al abrirse, una pantalla dibuja enseguida lo que no depende del servidor: los textos fijos, los títulos, el cuervo, las etiquetas y las pestañas. Un número que sale de los datos, como la cantidad de cada pestaña de filtro de Usuarios, no se muestra hasta que llegan. Cada tarjeta que espera datos se ve como un skeleton: un solo bloque gris, suave, con la forma y el tamaño de la tarjeta, sin nada adentro. Una tarjeta es la unidad que el usuario reconoce: la sesión destacada, cada card de una sección plegable, cada card de encuesta, cada fila de una lista, la slide, el nombre y el avatar del header. El skeleton nunca dibuja el contenido interno de una tarjeta, como sus textos, botones o íconos. La web trata el chequeo del login como un dato más de la pantalla que se abre. Mientras la web espera la respuesta, el nombre y el avatar del header se ven en skeleton. Cuando llegan los datos, cada parte los muestra. El aula del estudiante necesita la lista de sesiones para saber qué sesión abrir. Mientras la lista llega, el aula se dibuja en skeleton: el título del header, la slide con los controles de debajo, y el contenido de cada pestaña del panel, con las pestañas fijas.

edits.newText:
El profe mueve la slide desde la pestaña Aula del admin de la sesión (1). Su web le dice a su HTML a qué `slide` y `step` ir (2) y le manda la nueva posición a la API (3), que la guarda en D1, en `current_slide` y `current_step` de la sesión (4) y le avisa al aula (5). El aula avisa a los conectados (6), cada web le pide la posición guardada a la API (7, 8), y la de quien sigue al profe lleva su HTML ahí (9) (ver [tiempo real del aula](tiempo-real-del-aula.md)).

La web del profe guarda una posición por vez. Si el profe sigue moviéndose mientras se guarda una, la web le muestra cada movimiento al instante y se queda solo con la última posición, que manda cuando responde el pedido anterior. Mientras guarda, la web del profe muestra su propia posición y no la que le devuelven la API o los avisos del aula. Cuando termina de guardar, vuelve a mostrar la posición guardada. Los estudiantes y la pestaña de presentar van directo a la última posición, sin pasar por las del medio. Si un pedido falla, aparece un toast y la web vuelve a la posición que tiene guardada la API.

> [!NOTE] Por qué el profe no manda cada movimiento
> Las respuestas y los avisos llegan con demora. Si la web mandara un pedido por movimiento y tomara cada respuesta, una respuesta vieja la devolvería a una posición anterior mientras el profe sigue avanzando, y el próximo movimiento saldría desde ahí. Guardar de a una posición y quedarse con la última manda menos pedidos y deja la pantalla donde el profe la llevó.

**Slides on the teacher side** (`TeacherSlides.tsx`, `useMoveSlide.ts`):
- The screen keeps its own position while moves are saving, so a late response or a refetch from the classroom notice can't move it back.
- Only one save is in flight at a time. If you move again while one is saving, it keeps only your last position and sends it when the pending save answers. When the last save lands, the screen goes back to showing the saved position.
- `useMoveSlide` no longer patches the cache or writes the response back. If a save fails, the toast still shows and the session is fetched again, so the screen goes back to what the API has.
- One new test clicks forward twice and back once while the first save is held. The screen follows every click, the first request stays the only one in flight, and when it answers only the last position is sent.

**Single skeleton on the featured card** (`routes/_app/index.tsx`, `FeaturedSession.tsx`):
- The card stays one skeleton until the sessions, the active polls and, when featured questions are on, the questions have arrived. Then it appears whole.
- `FeaturedSession` now receives the questions as data. I removed `FeaturedQuestions.tsx`, which only switched between its own skeleton and the card.
- One new test holds the questions back: only the skeleton shows, then the full card appears with its questions.

**Docs:**
- `api-de-las-slides.md` describes the new slide behaviour and why the web doesn't send every move.
- `carga-y-acciones-de-la-web.md` says that a card made of several parts waits for all of them, and that moving the slide saves one position at a time.

Should I commit them as two commits, one per change, on this branch?

content.text:
---
name: "agentic-review"
description: "Refines the code in a change before a human reads it. Runs four facet reviewers and one conventions reviewer per wiki entry and per project rule file on each repository, fixes what they find without changing how the change looks or behaves, and repeats for up to three rounds. Typed by the user, or invoked by mahou:implement once a repository's code lands."
---
Load mahou:basics first. Then read `.mahou/agentic-review.md` if present.

# Agentic review

Cleans up a change so mahou:human-review spends its attention on judgment instead of on mechanical findings. It reviews for reuse, simplification, efficiency, altitude, and conformance to the conventions the wiki holds.

It does not look for correctness bugs. Those belong to the human pass, where someone can weigh whether the behavior was intended.

## Fixing without asking

`basics` says every decision belongs to the user and every choice goes back to them as a question. This skill is the exception, and it holds inside these bounds:

- It fixes nothing that would change how the change looks or behaves.
- It keeps every mechanism that a settled program design entry, a settled design tree leaf, an explicit user decision or a source on the conventions list chose. A prototype settles how the change looks and behaves, not how it is coded, so the review may change code that does what the prototype's code did in a different way.
- It may create a new file or edit a file the changeset does not touch when the fix reduces complexity or duplication, or otherwise improves the code.
- It leaves everything uncommitted, so the user can read the whole pass with one `git diff` and discard it as a whole.
- It reports every fix and every skip.

A finding whose fix would break any of those becomes a skipped finding in the report, for the user to rule on.

## Step 1: Establish the changeset

Load mahou:changeset for the repositories, the base, and the diff.

Then settle the conventions list, the sources the conventions reviewers check the change against. When the caller passes one, use it as given. When it does not, follow the wiki indexes, global and local, to the entries about the technologies the diff touches, and add the project's `CLAUDE.md` and `.mahou/basics.md` when present. Open every source on the list. Every fix has to follow them.

## Step 2: Dispatch the facet reviewers

Per repository, one reviewer per facet and one conventions reviewer per source on the list, all in a single message so they run together.

| Facet | Agent | Looks for |
|---|---|---|
| Reuse | `mahou:reuse-reviewer` | new code re-implementing something the codebase already has |
| Simplification | `mahou:simplification-reviewer` | redundant or derivable state, copy-paste with variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind |
| Efficiency | `mahou:efficiency-reviewer` | redundant computation, repeated I/O, independent work run sequentially, closures pinning large scopes |
| Altitude | `mahou:altitude-reviewer` | special cases layered on shared infrastructure where the mechanism underneath should generalize instead |
| Conventions | `mahou:conventions-reviewer`, one per source | departures from the one wiki entry or rule file it is given |

Give each one the repository's absolute path, the base, the diff, and the path to write its findings to. Give each conventions reviewer the path of its source as well, and a findings path of its own.

Reviewers write findings to that file and return the path and a count. Nothing comes back in the message body, which truncates long reports and costs a round trip to recover.

Every round spawns fresh reviewers; never resume one from an earlier round. A reviewer that has seen its own last report defends it and repeats what was skipped, and a reviewer resumed per facet only hears about its own fixes, so it can undo what another facet fixed. From the second round on, give every reviewer the ledger (Step 4) as well.

## Step 3: Apply what came back

Read every findings file. Collapse findings that different facets raised about the same line or mechanism, then fix each survivor.

Skip a finding when its fix would change intended behavior, reach outside the bounds above, or when you judge it a false positive. Record the skip with why the reviewer proposed the change, the problem the reviewer saw in the code, and why you skipped the finding. Never argue with it.

Then read every comment the diff adds, yourself, against the project's comments rule: a wiki entry, the project's `CLAUDE.md` or a rule file in the repository. The reviewers do not flag comments. Remove or rewrite every comment the rule does not allow. When the project states no comments rule, say so and leave the comments as they are.

Run the repository's linters and tests afterwards, scoped to the files you touched rather than the whole tree. The project's `CLAUDE.md` usually names the commands; when it does not, detect them from the lockfile or manifest and say which you ran.

## Step 4: Record the round and show it

Keep one ledger per repository at `agentic-review/<repo>.md` in the change's scratch folder. At the end of each round, append a section for the round with every fix applied (file, line, the facet that raised it, what changed) and every skip with its reason, then the linter and test results.

Show the user the round's status: per repository the count of fixes and skips, one line per fix, each skip with its reason, and the checks' result. Then start the next round without waiting for an answer.

## Step 5: Round again, up to three times

Run Step 2 again with fresh reviewers and the ledger. Tell each reviewer:

- Every fix in the ledger is settled. Do not propose reverting or reshaping one, unless the fix itself introduced a problem on your angle; then cite the ledger entry.
- Every skip in the ledger is settled. Do not raise it again.
- Report only what still stands on your angle in the current diff.

When applying the round's findings, drop any finding that reverses a ledger fix or repeats a ledger skip, and record it as dropped in the round's section.

Stop when a round returns no findings that survive, or after the third round, whichever comes first.

## Step 6: Report and hand off

Per repository: what each round fixed, what it skipped, and the linter and test results, with the ledger path. Write each skipped finding so the user can rule on it without asking back: the problem the reviewer saw and why the reviewer proposed the change, then why the review skipped the finding. Everything stays uncommitted.

Then hand off to mahou:human-review.

`@kurasu/slides/navigation` already exports the identical `samePosition`
(`app/packages/slides/src/navigation.ts:25`), and `StudentSlides.tsx:3` imports it from there

## 1. TeacherSlides repeats the "save finished" reset in two places

# Efficiency review, round 1

Findings: 2 (both low severity). No hot-path, memory or request-count regressions.

## 1. Featured card waits on the slowest of three requests (low)

`app/apps/web/src/routes/_app/index.tsx:38-46`

Polls and questions start in parallel once `sessions` resolves, so there is no extra waterfall. Time to first card is now max(polls, questions) after sessions, where before the card was partly visible earlier. This is the requested behavior; it costs perceived latency, not extra requests. No change needed unless the polls or questions endpoint is slow in practice.

## 2. Failed polls or questions query leaves the skeleton up (low)

`app/apps/web/src/routes/_app/index.tsx:43-45`

`isFeaturedLoading` depends on `data == null`. If `activePolls` or `questions` errors after retries, `data` stays undefined and the card stays a skeleton, while the previous code showed the card without that part. Not a request-count issue, but it keeps the skeleton rendered indefinitely. Consider also checking `isPending` (or `isError`) instead of `data == null`.

## Checked, no issue

- `TeacherSlides.tsx`: serial save with last-wins coalescing sends at most one in-flight request plus one follow-up, fewer requests than one per move. `setMoving` per click is a cheap re-render. Final `cancelQueries` + `setQueryData` replaces the previous per-move write-back, so cache writes dropped from N to 1.
- `useMoveSlide.ts`: removing the optimistic patch removes a snapshot/cancel/patch cycle per move. Failure invalidates one exact key, once.
- `useQuestionsByVotes` options spread: new object per render, but `useApiQuery` already receives a fresh object each render elsewhere; `select: byVotes` is a stable module reference, so no select re-runs.
- `enabled: student && isWithQuestions` with key `""` for no featured session: query is disabled, no fetch.
- Skeleton branch builds `FeaturedSession` with static example data; no extra queries.

## 1. The save queue lives inside the TeacherSlides component
`app/apps/web/src/features/classroom/TeacherSlides.tsx:25-75`

The component holds a hand-rolled state machine: two refs, recursive `save`, a `.then/.catch` chain, a `cancelQueries` + `setQueryData` write-back, and a `moving` state. The component is also meant to render slides and wire `onNavigate`. The queue logic (serialize, keep last, show own position until idle) is a separate concern from drawing, and it is sized like a hook (`useSerializedMoves(session)` returning `{ position, navigate }`). The project rule is one function per module unless highly cohesive, and this is a second function with its own state sitting in a component file. ## 2. Cache responsibility moved up a layer, and the layers now disagree
`useMoveSlide.ts` (whole file) vs `TeacherSlides.tsx:48-55`

Before, `useMoveSlide` owned the cache (optimistic patch, write-back). Now the hook's comment says it "touches no cache" but still invalidates on error, while the component reaches into `useQueryClient` and `queryKeys.adminSession` to cancel and write the saved session. Cache handling for one key is split across two modules at two levels: the failure path is in the hook (`onError` invalidate), the success path is in the component, and the component's `.catch` resets state a second time. A reader has to read both to know what happens to `adminSession` after a move. Put both paths in one place (the extracted hook from finding 1, or the mutation hook), and have the component know neither the client nor the key.

## 3. The home route carries the featured card's loading logic and a placeholder id
`app/apps/web/src/routes/_app/index.tsx:38-47, 55-75`

The route now owns the questions query, the `isWithQuestions` flag, the "card is loading" aggregate across three queries, and two near-identical `<FeaturedSession>` renders (skeleton and real) that must be kept in sync by hand. Previously each part loaded inside the card's own components. The aggregation belongs at the card level (for example `useFeaturedCard(featured)` returning `{ isLoading, polls, questions }`, or a `FeaturedSessionLoader` component that renders skeleton or card), leaving the route to choose among skeleton, empty, and list. "", { enabled })` passes an empty string as a session id so a hook can be called before `featured` exists; it is a fake value at a call site that should not need one, and a hook scoped to the featured card would avoid it.

# Findings: operation-hooks convention

## 1. TeacherSlides writes the cache itself
- File: app/apps/web/src/features/classroom/TeacherSlides.tsx (`save`, the `.then` after `mutateAsync`)
- Convention: a mutation hook declares what it invalidates or writes with `setQueryData`; screens only call the hooks.
- The screen calls `useQueryClient`, `cancelQueries` and `setQueryData(queryKeys.adminSession(...), saved)`. Before the change that write lived in `useMoveSlide.onSuccess`. Moving it into the screen splits the operation's cache handling between the hook and its caller, and the screen now imports `queryKeys`.
- Fix direction: keep the write-back in `useMoveSlide` (its own `onSuccess`). Cancel/skip it when another move is pending, or have the hook accept the queue state through `options`. The screen then keeps only its local position and queue.

## 2. useMoveSlide's success path no longer settles the cache
- File: app/apps/web/src/features/sessions/useMoveSlide.ts
- Convention: the hook declares an invalidation or a `setQueryData` for what the operation changes.
- After the change the hook declares nothing on success, only an invalidation on error. A caller that uses `useMoveSlide` without TeacherSlides's extra code leaves `adminSession` stale. The hook's own comment says it "touches no cache", which makes the hook incomplete as the single place for the operation.
- Fix direction: same as finding 1; the hook should write or invalidate `queryKeys.adminSession(id)` on success.

# Simplification · round 2

## 1. `HomeFeaturedSession.tsx`: `session.featuredQuestions` se evalúa cuatro veces

`app/apps/web/src/features/sessions/HomeFeaturedSession.tsx` repite `session.featuredQuestions` en la condición de espera, en las preguntas del skeleton, en las de la card y en `enabled`. La condición compuesta `polls.data == null || (session.featuredQuestions && questions.data == null)` y los dos ternarios `featuredQuestions ? x : undefined` se simplifican con una sola lectura:

- `const withQuestions = session.featuredQuestions;` y usarla en `enabled`, en la espera y en los dos ternarios.

No hay que sacar el ternario de la card real: con `enabled: false` y datos de la sesión en el cache (por ejemplo, los del aula) `questions.data` puede traer preguntas aunque la sesión no las destaque.

Cambio chico; sin otros hallazgos en el diff actual (`useSlideMoves`, `useMoveSlide`, `FeaturedSession`, `useQuestionsByVotes` y los docs quedan como están).
######## altitude
# Round 2 · altitude · kurasu

## 1. Dos skeletons de la misma card en dos niveles, con contenido distinto

`app/apps/web/src/routes/_app/index.tsx:35-39` dibuja el skeleton de `FeaturedSession` con `sessionExamples[2]` y `polls={[]}` mientras cargan las sesiones. `app/apps/web/src/features/sessions/HomeFeaturedSession.tsx:20-26` dibuja otro skeleton de la misma card con `pollExamples[0]` y, si corresponde, `questionExamples`, mientras cargan encuestas y preguntas. La card queda con dos skeletons de tamaño distinto en cargas consecutivas, y el usuario pidió un solo skeleton hasta que llega todo. Cuando las sesiones llegan, la altura salta de la card sin encuestas ni preguntas a la card con ambas. La decisión "qué se ve de la card destacada mientras carga" está repartida entre la ruta y `HomeFeaturedSession`.

Corrección: que el skeleton de la card viva solo en `HomeFeaturedSession` (o en un componente de la card) con el mismo contenido de ejemplo, y que la ruta lo use para el caso `sessions.data == null` en vez de armar el suyo.

## 2. `session.featuredQuestions` se decide tres veces en `HomeFeaturedSession`

`app/apps/web/src/features/sessions/HomeFeaturedSession.tsx:17-34` consulta `session.featuredQuestions` en el `enabled` del hook, en la condición del skeleton y en cada `questions=` de las dos ramas. `FeaturedSession` recibe luego `questions` como `undefined` para significar "la card no muestra preguntas", así que la bandera de la sesión se traduce a un dato opcional y se vuelve a leer arriba. El nivel de la regla ("la card muestra preguntas") está mezclado con el de la carga.

Corrección: calcular la regla una vez en el componente (por ejemplo `const questionsData = session.featuredQuestions ? questions.data : undefined` y esperar con una sola condición) y reutilizarla en las dos ramas.
######## reuse
# Round 2 · reuse

## Findings

1. `app/apps/web/src/features/classroom/useSlideMoves.ts:56` builds `{ slide: session.currentSlide, step: session.currentStep }` inline. The same expression already exists in `PresentedSlides.tsx:16` and `StudentSlides.tsx:33`, so the change adds a third copy. Extract a helper next to `samePosition` (for example `positionOf(session)` in `@kurasu/slides/navigation`, or a function in `features/classroom/`) and use it in the three places. Low severity.

No other findings: `samePosition`, `SkeletonOf`, the example fixtures (`pollExamples`, `questionExamples`), `FeaturedQuestionsCard` and `useQuestions` (through the extended `useQuestionsByVotes`) are reused rather than duplicated.

I'm looking at a state-driven alternative: an effect that watches the mutation's pending flag and the current waiting position, saving whenever the mutation is idle and the position differs from the last one saved. The mutation's pending flag only flips after a delayed notify, so there's a small window where two saves could overlap. **Verdict: Partly.** The mutation state can replace `isSaving`. It can't replace `waiting`, and `moving` stays as state. Both refs came in with this change.

**`isSaving` (line 17): Confirmed.** It repeats what `move.isPending` already says. The ref exists because of a timing gap, not because the information is missing:

- **The gap:** React Query reports a mutation's status to the component through `notifyManager`, which batches with `setTimeout(callback, 0)` (`query-core/notifyManager.js:5`). Right after `mutate()`, `move.isPending` is still `false` until the component re-renders.
- **Why it doesn't matter here:** each click is a separate event, and React renders between two clicks, so by the second click `isPending` is already `true`.
- **Where it could matter:** in the chain inside `.then()`, where `save(next)` starts the next request immediately. At that moment `isPending` can still read the previous render's value. That's harmless as long as `navigate` is the only reader and it reads on a later click.

So `isSaving` can go, and `navigate` asks `move.isPending` instead.

**`waiting` (line 18): Not a bug.** The mutation state can't hold this:

- **What it holds:** the position the teacher moves to while a save is in flight, which hasn't been sent yet. `move.variables` only holds the position already sent.
- **Why it's a ref, not state:** `.then()` reads it when the save answers. A `useState` would be stale there, because that closure belongs to the render that started the save. A ref always gives the latest value.
- **The alternative:** React Query can run mutations one after another with `scope`. Then each click queues its own request and `waiting` disappears. But that sends every intermediate position, which you ruled out when you chose to keep only the last one.

**`moving` (line 16) stays as state:** it's the position the screen shows, so it has to cause a re-render.

**What the change would be:** remove `isSaving`, use `move.isPending` in `navigate`, and keep `waiting` as a ref. Should I make that change?

**How it works:**
- **What it keeps:** a single `useState`, `unsavedPosition`. It holds where the teacher moved and the server hasn't confirmed yet. Whether a save is running and what it sent are read from `moveMutation` (`isPending`, `variables`).
- **When it sends:** an effect sends `unsavedPosition` when no save is running and that position hasn't been sent yet. If you click several times during a save, only the last position goes out when the save answers.
- **When the screen goes back to the saved session:** when the last save sent exactly `unsavedPosition`, or when it failed. This is computed during render, not stored.
- **`navigate`:** it resets the mutation when no save is running.

**Two things changed from what I proposed:**
- **No `setState` in the effect:** the lint rule `react/set-state-in-effect` rejects it, so "the save is done" is computed during render instead of clearing the state.
- **The reset in `navigate`:** without it, moving back to the position you saved last would match what the mutation last sent, and that position would never be sent again.

The caveat from before still applies: two clicks in the same tick, before React re-renders, could send two requests in parallel. Separate clicks never get that close.

Should I commit it as two commits on `feat/session-4-deck`, one per change?
